edge.title: The strip that looks right
edge.setup: You need a course of antibiotics, or a regular medicine for someone at home. An online listing or a small shop offers it noticeably cheaper than the chemist you normally use. The strip looks right, the box looks right, and the seller is cheerful about it. You have no way to read what is inside.
edge.tell: The price is below what every other chemist charges, or the seller cannot give you a bill showing the batch number.
move: Buy prescription medicines only from a licensed chemist, and ask for a printed bill that carries the batch number and expiry date.
Check that the batch number and expiry on the bill match what is printed on the strip and the outer box. A mismatch, smudged print or a re-stuck label means you stop there.
If a price is far below the going rate, treat it as the finding, not as a bargain. Compare it against a second licensed chemist before you buy.
If a medicine seems wrong or does nothing, keep the packaging and the bill and report it to the state drugs control department; do not throw the evidence away.
edge.why: You cannot verify a medicine yourself, so you rely on signals that are cheap to fake: the packaging, the brand name, a confident seller. The only part a counterfeiter cannot fake cheaply is a paper trail that runs back to a licensed supplier, and a price that makes sense. The mechanism is that the buyer knows least at the moment of purchase, and the seller knows exactly what is in the box. So you demand the one thing that moves information to your side: a bill with a batch number.
edge.variants: Same shape: counterfeit supplements and protein powder, refilled branded cosmetics, 'original' spare parts for a car or phone, re-sealed bottled water or cooking oil, a cheap 'sealed' phone with no invoice.

scenario.question: Someone at home needs a five-day course of antibiotics. An online listing offers the same brand at about 40% below what your usual chemist charges, with delivery tonight. The photo shows the right strip and box. The seller says a bill is 'not needed for this item'. What do you do?

choices.text: Buy from a licensed chemist who gives a printed bill with the batch number and expiry, and check that both match the strip and the box before you open it.
Order it. The packaging in the photo matches the brand exactly, so it must be genuine.
Order it and keep the delivery screenshot as proof in case it does not work.
Order it, but compare the strip against an old one at home when it arrives before deciding to use it.

lens.name: Fixed costs
lens.one_line: When most of the cost does not move with use, more use does not fix the books quickly.
lens.detail: Costs come in two kinds: those that rise with every unit sold (fuel, ingredients, a driver's shift) and those owed regardless (loan repayments, interest, rent, depreciation). When the second kind dominates, growth in customers helps only slowly, and anything that raises the fixed part, such as a rate rise or a weaker rupee on a foreign loan, can swamp it. Before concluding that more users will rescue something, ask where the money actually goes.
elsewhere: A car whose EMI, insurance and parking cost the same whether you drive it twice a month or daily, so the real question is the cost per trip.
A restaurant full every night that still shuts because its rent was fixed at the peak.
A household where the home-loan EMI, not the grocery bill, decides how badly a pay cut hurts.
lens.test: Which of these costs would still be owed if usage doubled, or halved?
lens.today: Prop News Time reports Namma Metro ridership grew 12.29 per cent while its loss before tax widened to ₹1,717 crore, and Construction World reports that exchange-rate losses pushed finance costs above revenue. More riders cannot outrun costs tied to loans and the rupee. When a system's loss sits on the finance side, the fixes on the table are usually fares, subsidies or refinancing, not footfall, so do not assume growing ridership will keep your fare where it is.

moved.what: Overnight rain waterlogged Bengaluru roads and disrupted morning traffic, DD News reports. The forecast puts today's rain chance at 87%.
moved.so_what: Leave earlier than usual this morning and again this evening, and avoid underpasses and low stretches that flooded overnight; they take hours to drain once the rain returns.

moved.what: Police have registered an FIR after an emailed bomb threat targeted Diljit Dosanjh's Bengaluru concert, and the show is under security watch, The New Indian Express and Moneycontrol report.
moved.so_what: If you are going, expect longer security checks: carry only what fits in your pockets, arrive early, and note two exits when you get in. Check the police traffic advisory for the venue before you leave.

moved.what: A toddler playing outside his home was run over and killed by a water tanker, The Hindu, The Times of India and Deccan Herald report.
moved.so_what: A loaded tanker on a narrow residential lane has blind spots large enough to hide a child. When one is delivering on your street, keep small children inside or holding your hand until it has left.

moved.what: Bengaluru plans to asphalt 2,300 km of roads by February and white-top another 130 km across 88 stretches, with ₹5,394 crore allocated, The Times of India reports.
moved.so_what: Expect lane closures and diversions on major roads through February. White-topping closes a stretch for weeks, not nights, so if your daily route is on the list, find your alternative now rather than on the first jammed morning.

moved.what: Trial runs have begun on the Blue Line Phase 2A stretch from KR Puram towards Mahadevapura, with completion targeted for mid-2027, Swarajya and Indian Infrastructure Magazine report.
moved.so_what: Trials are not an opening. If you commute along the Outer Ring Road, plan for at least another eighteen months of road travel, and treat any rent premium for 'upcoming Metro' accordingly.

carry_over.prompt: A caller from 'your bank' knows your name, your card's last four digits and a recent bill, and says an OTP is coming to verify it is really you. What is the tell?
carry_over.answer: Anyone asking you to read out a code is, by definition, not your bank.
